::: {.objectives}
**Goals.** Write a correlated random walk simulator from scratch; watch
straightness emerge as persistence grows; find the ballistic–diffusive
crossover in mean squared displacement; add a bias and simulate homing;
discover why a power-law fit is not evidence of a Lévy walk; test whether real
buffalo are range-resident against a simulated null.

**Time:** ~70 minutes. **Packages:** `circular`, `amt`, `dplyr`, `ggplot2`.
:::

```{r}
library(circular)
library(amt)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Task 1 — A correlated random walk, from scratch

Three ingredients: step lengths (gamma), turning angles (von Mises), and a
running sum. Write it before you look at the solution.

```{r}
#| eval: false
simulate_crw <- function(n, shape = 2, scale = 250, kappa = 2) {
  # 1. draw n - 1 turning angles from a von Mises centred on 0
  # 2. heading = cumulative sum of turns, starting from 0
  # 3. draw n step lengths from a gamma
  # 4. x and y = cumulative sums of step * cos(heading), step * sin(heading)
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
rvm <- function(n, mu = 0, kappa = 1) {
  a <- as.numeric(rvonmises(n, circular(mu), kappa))   # circular -> plain numbers
  atan2(sin(a), cos(a))                                 # wrap to (-pi, pi]
}

simulate_crw <- function(n, shape = 2, scale = 250, kappa = 2) {
  turn    <- rvm(n - 1, 0, kappa)
  heading <- cumsum(c(0, turn))
  sl      <- rgamma(n, shape = shape, scale = scale)
  data.frame(step = seq_len(n),
             x = cumsum(sl * cos(heading)),
             y = cumsum(sl * sin(heading)),
             sl = sl)
}

set.seed(42)
simulate_crw(5)
```

Two traps worth knowing. `circular::rvonmises()` returns a `circular` object
that misbehaves in ordinary arithmetic — convert it with `as.numeric()`. And
its values lie in $[0, 2\pi)$, so wrap them to $(-\pi, \pi]$ before treating
them as turns left and right.

The finished version of this function, and the others in this practical,
lives in `R/simulators.R`. Sessions 6 and 7 `source()` that file.
:::

## Task 2 — Persistence makes straightness

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(1)
kappas <- c(0, 1, 3, 10)

sims <- lapply(kappas, function(k) {
  bind_rows(lapply(1:20, function(i) simulate_crw(200, kappa = k)), .id = "sim") |>
    mutate(kappa = k)
}) |> bind_rows()

ggplot(sims, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000, group = sim)) +
  geom_path(alpha = 0.3, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  facet_wrap(~ paste("κ =", kappa), nrow = 1) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "km", y = "km", title = "Twenty 200-step walks at each κ") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Your turn

**2a.** Compute the straightness index (net displacement / path length) for
each walk and summarise it by κ.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
sims |>
  group_by(kappa, sim) |>
  summarise(net = sqrt(last(x)^2 + last(y)^2), path = sum(sl), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(kappa) |>
  summarise(median_straightness = round(median(net / path), 3))
```

Straightness rises steeply with κ. But even at κ = 10 it is well below 1 over
200 steps: small turns accumulate, and a long enough correlated walk always
ends up wandering. Straightness is a property of the walk **and** of the
number of steps you measure it over.
:::

## Task 3 — Mean squared displacement

```{r}
msd <- function(d, lags) {
  sapply(lags, function(L)
    mean((d$x[-(1:L)] - head(d$x, -L))^2 + (d$y[-(1:L)] - head(d$y, -L))^2))
}

lags <- 2^(0:8)
set.seed(2)
msd_tab <- lapply(c(0, 2, 10), function(k) {
  m <- rowMeans(sapply(1:30, function(i) msd(simulate_crw(2000, kappa = k), lags)))
  data.frame(kappa = k, lag = lags, msd = m)
}) |> bind_rows()
```

### Your turn

**3a.** Plot MSD against lag on log–log axes.
**3b.** Estimate the slope at short lags (1–4) and at long lags (64–256).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(msd_tab, aes(lag, msd, colour = factor(kappa))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Lag (steps)", y = "MSD (m²)", colour = "κ") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
msd_tab |>
  group_by(kappa) |>
  summarise(
    slope_short = coef(lm(log(msd[lag <= 4]) ~ log(lag[lag <= 4])))[2],
    slope_long  = coef(lm(log(msd[lag >= 64]) ~ log(lag[lag >= 64])))[2]
  ) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("slope"), \(z) round(z, 2)))
```

The uncorrelated walk (κ = 0) has slope 1 at every lag: diffusive throughout.
Persistent walks start **ballistic** (slope approaching 2: they keep going
straight) and relax towards **diffusive** (slope 1) once they have forgotten
their heading. The more persistent the walk, the later the crossover — at
κ = 10 it has not quite finished even after 256 steps.

On a real track, the lag at which the slope drops from ~2 to ~1 estimates how
long the animal holds its direction. A slope that drops towards **0** means
something a random walk cannot do: the animal stops getting further away.
:::

## Task 4 — Bias: homing and central places

```{r}
source("R/simulators.R")   # simulate_bcrw() and friends
args(simulate_bcrw)
```

In `simulate_bcrw()`, each new heading is centred on a weighted circular mean
of the previous heading and the bearing to `goal`; `w` is the weight on the
goal.

### Your turn

**4a.** Release an animal 10 km from home. How many steps does it take to come
within 500 m, for `w` = 0.05, 0.1, 0.3?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
steps_to_home <- function(w, n = 3000) {
  d <- simulate_bcrw(n, goal = c(0, 0), w = w, kappa = 2, start = c(10000, 0))
  hit <- which(sqrt(d$x^2 + d$y^2) < 500)
  if (length(hit)) hit[1] else NA
}

set.seed(3)
homing <- lapply(c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3), function(w)
  data.frame(w = w, steps = replicate(50, steps_to_home(w)))) |>
  bind_rows()

homing |>
  group_by(w) |>
  summarise(median_steps = median(steps, na.rm = TRUE),
            failed = sum(is.na(steps)))
```

With the weakest bias, nearly half the walkers are still lost after 3,000
steps; doubling it gets almost all of them home, and a strong bias does it in
a few dozen steps. The weak-bias walkers wander a long way first: over a short
stretch you would not see the bias at all.
:::

**4b.** Keep the goal at the start point and run the walker for a long time.
What emerges?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-align: center
truth <- truth_animal()     # a central-place BCRW, 5,000 steps, fixed seed
ggplot(truth, aes(x / 1000, y / 1000)) +
  geom_path(colour = "#1f6f78", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.6) +
  annotate("point", x = 0, y = 0, colour = "firebrick", size = 3, shape = 17) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "km", y = "km", title = "A home range, from one movement rule") +
  theme_minimal()
```

A **home range**. Nothing in the rule mentions an area: the animal simply
wanders, with a slight pull towards home. The boundary emerges.

This is our **ground-truth animal**. Because we wrote the rule, we can
simulate it for as long as we like and know its true utilisation
distribution — so in Session 6 we can check which home-range estimator
recovers it.
:::

## Task 5 — Is it a Lévy walk?

Fit two models to step lengths above a threshold `xmin`, by maximum
likelihood: a (shifted) exponential and a power law (Pareto). Both have one
parameter, so AIC compares them fairly.

```{r}
compare_tails <- function(x, xmin) {
  x <- x[x >= xmin]
  n <- length(x)
  # power law: f(x) = (a - 1) / xmin * (x / xmin)^-a
  s <- sum(log(x / xmin))
  a <- 1 + n / s
  ll_pow <- n * log(a - 1) - n * log(xmin) - a * s
  # exponential shifted to start at xmin
  lambda <- 1 / (mean(x) - xmin)
  ll_exp <- n * log(lambda) - lambda * sum(x - xmin)
  data.frame(n = n, mu_hat = round(a, 2),
             AIC_exponential = round(2 - 2 * ll_exp),
             AIC_power_law   = round(2 - 2 * ll_pow),
             winner = ifelse(ll_pow > ll_exp, "power law", "exponential"))
}
```

### Your turn

**5a.** Test it on data where you know the answer: 2,000 exponential steps, and
2,000 power-law steps with μ = 2.
**5b.** Now 2,000 steps from an animal that switches between two behaviours,
each with *exponential* steps: 75% short (mean 60 m) and 25% long (mean
1,500 m).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{r}
set.seed(4)
bind_rows(
  cbind(data = "exponential",            compare_tails(rexp(2000, 1 / 300) + 50, 50)),
  cbind(data = "power law, mu = 2",      compare_tails(50 * runif(2000)^(-1), 50)),
  cbind(data = "two exponential modes",  compare_tails(c(rexp(1500, 1 / 60),
                                                         rexp(500, 1 / 1500)) + 10, 10))
)
```

The method gets the first two right. But the **mixture of two exponentials** —
two ordinary random walks, no power law anywhere — is "identified" as a power
law, decisively. That is Benhamou's (2007) point: a heavy-tailed step-length
distribution is what you get whenever an animal switches between short-step
and long-step behaviours.

A power-law fit describes the **shape** of the distribution. It cannot tell
you the **process**. To claim a Lévy strategy you must first rule out that the
long steps belong to a separate behavioural state — which is what the hidden
Markov models of Session 8 are for.
:::

## Task 6 — Is a buffalo range-resident? A simulation test

Null hypothesis: the buffalo moves like a correlated random walk with its
**own** step-length and turning-angle distributions, and no memory of place.
Statistic: the **radius of gyration** of its longest continuous burst — the
root-mean-square distance of its positions from their centre.

```{r}
buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier, t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(buffalo, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

radius_of_gyration <- function(x, y) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2 + (y - mean(y))^2)) / 1000

null_test <- function(animal, n_sim = 300) {
  hourly <- trk |>
    filter(id == animal) |>
    track_resample(rate = lubridate::hours(1), tolerance = lubridate::minutes(10)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  st <- hourly |> steps_by_burst() |> filter(sl_ > 0, sl_ < 10000)
  g  <- fit_distr(st$sl_, "gamma")                          # the animal's own steps
  vm <- fit_distr(st$ta_[!is.na(st$ta_)], "vonmises")       # and its own turns
  longest <- hourly |> filter(burst_ == names(which.max(table(burst_))))
  n <- nrow(longest)
  obs <- radius_of_gyration(longest$x_, longest$y_)
  sim <- replicate(n_sim, {
    d <- simulate_crw(n, shape = g$params$shape, scale = g$params$scale,
                      kappa = vm$params$kappa)
    radius_of_gyration(d$x, d$y)
  })
  data.frame(id = animal, burst_days = round(n / 24), observed_km = round(obs, 1),
             null_median_km = round(median(sim), 1),
             percentile = round(100 * mean(sim < obs)))
}

set.seed(7)
null_test("Cilla")
```

### Your turn

**6a.** Is Cilla more confined than a random walk?
**6b.** Run the test on all six buffalo, and plot the percentile against burst
length. What do you learn?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

Cilla's radius of gyration is smaller than the simulated median, but about a
third of the random walks are more compact still (the exact share varies a
little from run to run). With 77 days of data we **cannot**
reject the null.

```{r}
set.seed(7)
all_tests <- bind_rows(lapply(unique(trk$id), null_test))
all_tests
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center
ggplot(all_tests, aes(burst_days, percentile, label = id)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(2.5, 50), linetype = c(2, 3), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f6f78") +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 5) +
  labs(x = "Length of continuous burst (days)",
       y = "Percentile within the CRW null",
       title = "Confinement shows only in long tracks") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Only Toni, with 157 days of continuous data, is clearly more confined than a
random walk. The others were tracked for weeks, not months, and over a few
weeks a resident and a random walker cover similar ground: the resident has
not yet had time to reach the edges of its range.

This is the **tracking duration versus occupation timescale** problem. It is
not a failure of the test; it is the test telling you your data are too short
to answer the question. Session 6's variogram diagnoses the same thing.
:::

## Self-check

::: {.quiz}
You simulate 1,000 CRWs as a null and your animal's statistic falls at the
40th percentile. What can you conclude?

- [ ] The animal is a correlated random walker
- [x] The data do not let you distinguish the animal from the null for this statistic
- [ ] The simulation was too small
- [ ] The animal is range-resident

::: {.quiz-feedback}
Failing to reject a null is not evidence that the null is true. The animal
might be doing something else entirely that this statistic cannot detect — or
the track may simply be too short. Report it as "consistent with", never as
"is".
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why must the null CRW use the animal's **own** fitted step and turn
distributions?

- [ ] To make the simulation faster
- [x] So that the null differs from the animal only in the mechanism being tested
- [ ] Because `simulate_crw()` requires them
- [ ] It does not matter which distributions you use

::: {.quiz-feedback}
If the null used shorter steps than the animal, the animal would look "less
confined" simply because it moves further per hour. A null must match the
animal in everything **except** the mechanism under test — here, memory of
place — or rejecting it tells you nothing.
:::
:::
